events.description: An engineer starts setting up multiple PostgreSQL servers in staging to try out pgpool-II for load balancing queries (infrastructure#259).
Prior to starting this work, the engineer takes an LVM snapshot of the production database and loads it into the staging environment to get a more up-to-date copy for load testing.

GitLab.com experiences a sharp increase in database load, suspected to be spam; many users cannot post comments on issues and merge requests, and getting load under control takes several hours. Part of the load is later found to come from a background job removing an employee's account accidentally scheduled for removal after being flagged for abuse.

Due to increased load, the PostgreSQL secondary's replication lags and fails because required WAL segments were already removed from the primary; with no WAL archiving, the secondary must be manually re-synchronised. An engineer wipes the secondary's data directory and runs pg_basebackup, which hangs silently and then reports that the primary lacks available replication connections.

events.time: After the pg_basebackup failures (around ± 23:00–23:30 UTC, January 31st)
events.description: Engineers temporarily raise max_wal_senders from 3 to 32; PostgreSQL refuses to restart due to too many semaphores, so max_connections is reduced from 8000 to 2000, allowing a successful restart. pg_basebackup still does not start replication, and strace shows it hanging in a poll call.

An engineer suspects pg_basebackup's earlier attempts created files in the secondary's data directory. While trying to restore replication, an engineer mistakenly wipes the PostgreSQL data directory on the primary instead of the secondary; the process is terminated a second or two later, but around 300 GB of data has already been removed.
Engineers look for database backups and ask for help on Slack; the process of finding and using backups fails completely.

GitLab.com's database is restored (without webhooks) from the LVM snapshot taken about 6 hours before the outage, as the best option to minimise data loss, a process that took roughly 18 hours of copying over slow disks.
Final restoration procedures are completed, including restoring webhooks and confirming everything operates as expected.
